items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1959-06-30
items.q: Around seventeen, I joined, Lee Collins' band. I went to Pensacola, Florida.

ctx.x: Who did Lloyd Arthur Dog play with?

He played with the Arnold Brass Band. They played first clarinet. He died young with a social disease. My great-aunt term. He was a shy boy. He was a basketball sergeant. Some sportswoman enticed him and got in a corral and contacted his disease. And they wouldn't tell the old folks that he was sick. And somehow they detected that he had this trouble. And when they found out about it and rushed him to the hospital, it was too late. So he died of this sickness. And this is just a lot on the planet. So Michael Paul…
Back to Florida for a minute. What were the bands like in Florida other than the band you were with?

items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: And I played with Lee Collins and them. That’s where I graduate to big time. I joined Lee Collins and David Jones’s band.

ctx.x: Wiggins. A great piano player. Played with him. And I played with Lee Collins and them. That’s where I graduate to big time. I joined Lee Collins and David Jones’s band. I taken [Emmanuel] Sayles’s place. They had scanned banjo players around there.

That’s why they called me to the rehearsal they had. Lee Collins look at me. I had on these $20 [? (inaudible)] shoes [? (inaudible)]. Later on he said, “You know why I hired you?” He said, “You wasn’t playing much banjo. I hired you because you had on them pretty shoes. I used to like to look at them shoes, and I knew you’d amount to something some day.” That’s why he hired me in the band. I went in the band and that’s where I heard some [expletive deleted]. Me, Roy . . . now who the hell was on bass?

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: And that's why Lee kept me. He said, "You straightened Ernest Kelly out."

ctx.x: And that's why Lee kept me. He said, "You straightened Ernest Kelly out." When I joined... They needed a banjo player, so they sent... They knew that I could play a little bit. They was always lookin'... Because a lot of... When you said, "I'm going on the road," a lot of musicians said, "I ain't going. Where are they going? It's going to be a bazah(?)," which mean ain't nothin' gonna happen. "So you're goin' out there? They ain't gonna make enough money. You're wastin' your time. 'Cause it ain't payday out there…

Now, (?) me, I wanted to...I would go anywhere, whether I get paid or not. This is a trip for me. I ain't gonna sulk and I'm not a big eater. So I could get me a slice of bread and some water, and make it -- and I don't care where it's at. And I wasn't afraid to go anywhere, because I could run like hell, and I figured if I got into trouble, if I could get in the woods, they ain't never gonna catch me. See? So I was never worried about going nowhere.

items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1976-02-04
items.q: I was with Lee Collins, Jones and Collins. Astoria Band.

ctx.x: Excuse me Danny, what was the name of the band you were with then?

I was with Lee Collins, Jones and Collins. Astoria Band. We played at Astoria. We played in New Orleans on Rampart Street which was owned by Beansy Furrier. It had once been owned by, I can't think of a man's name. It was a brewery people. Beansy took it over. It was a gambling concession. and we worked there. And Professor Cook was the emcee in musical and performance director and everything. He was the wheel around there. So he staged this train excursion to Chicago, and we had our band to play.
